title: Felix and the Drop
premise: Orsen Montrose has spent nine years as a ghost inside the Financial Integrity Unit, laundering nothing and investigating everything, living in a government safe house under a name that isn't his. When the safe house is quietly listed for sale online — complete with interior photos showing his life in forensic detail — Orsen realizes someone inside the system sold him out, and that the photographs are a message: come trade, or be found. The secret at stake is a ledger he copied years ago from his first case, one naming the officials who built the clean-money pipeline he's been hunting ever since. As buyers, brokers, and the colleague he trusted most converge on the sale, Orsen must decide whether to burn the ledger, sell it, or use it to buy himself a family among the strangers who help him run. In the end he trades the ledger for evidence that dismantles the pipeline, testifies under his real name, and chooses an ordinary, visible life with the people who refused to let him disappear.
about_author: Elodie Montrose is the pen name of a former compliance analyst who spent a decade tracing money she was never allowed to talk about. She writes thrillers about paper trails, quiet betrayals, and the people who live between the lines of official records.

chapters.title: The House That Isn't His
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. A routine morning in the safe house shatters when he finds the property listed on a real-estate site, interior photos including his unmade bed, his wall of case clippings, the ledger's hiding spot blurred but recognizable. Emotional beat: the vertigo of realizing invisibility was always rented, never owned.

chapters.title: Clean Money
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV, flashback woven through present. He walks into the Unit, where his caseload is deliberately boring — cases designed to fail, money designed to look innocent. He begins quietly checking who had access to safe-house records. Beat: paranoia sharpening into method.

chapters.title: Nine Years of Nobody
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. He reviews the rules of his witness arrangement with his handler, Dana Voss: no photos, no attachments, no real name. Dana insists the listing is a clerical error. Her reassurance lands wrong. Beat: the loneliness of a man whose only relationship is procedural.

chapters.title: The Blurred Rectangle
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. He retrieves the ledger from its hiding place — pages copied from his first case, the Halvern file, naming three officials who laundered billions through shell charities. The listing photo shows exactly where it sat. Beat: understanding this was never an accident; it's an invitation.

chapters.title: Nadia at the End of the Street
chapters.summary: Nadia Okonkwo's POV introduced. A retired schoolteacher and neighborhood watch organizer who has noticed 'the quiet man' for years, she spots a stranger photographing houses and calls it in. Beat: warmth entering the story from outside Orsen's sealed world.

chapters.title: Buyers
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. An encrypted message arrives via the listing's inquiry form: an offer to buy the house — and everything in it. The sender knows the ledger exists. Beat: fear converting to leverage; Orsen realizes he holds something they want.

chapters.title: The Halvern File
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV, extended flashback. Nine years earlier: his first investigation, the young official who died before testifying, and the moment Orsen copied the ledger instead of filing it. Beat: guilt revealed — his invisibility began as a choice that cost someone else everything.

chapters.title: Tea and Surveillance
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Nadia invites Orsen for tea under the pretext of neighborhood safety; he goes against every rule and finds himself talking — almost honestly — for the first time in years. Beat: the dangerous comfort of being seen by someone harmless.

chapters.title: Dana's Signature
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. He traces the listing back through escrow paperwork and finds Dana's digital signature on the disclosure documents. Either she sold him out or someone used her credentials. Beat: betrayal as ambiguity; trust becomes a liability.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Unit
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. He confronts Dana after hours. She admits the listing went up over her objection — someone above her is flushing him out because the pipeline investigation is getting warm. She gives him forty-eight hours before she's ordered to hand him over. Beat: ally and captor in the same body.

chapters.title: The Open House
chapters.summary: Multi-POV. The listed house holds an open house; Nadia volunteers as a greeter while Orsen watches from across the street. Three visitors aren't buyers: a broker for the syndicate, an internal-affairs officer, and someone from Orsen's past. Beat: the trap closing in broad daylight.

chapters.title: Run
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. He evacuates the safe house with minutes to spare, taking only the ledger, and Nadia hides him in her garage when the street fills with cars. Beat: terror braided with gratitude — found family forming under pressure.

chapters.title: What Nadia Knows
chapters.summary: Nadia's POV. She reveals she recognized him years ago — his face was in a newspaper photo from the Halvern era — and said nothing, choosing to let him be whoever he needed to be. Beat: belonging offered without conditions, which terrifies Orsen more than the hunters do.

chapters.title: The Third Name
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Studying the ledger, he realizes the third named official is now the deputy director overseeing his own protection detail. The people guarding him are the people he can prove guilty. Beat: the walls of the maze revealed as the maze itself.

chapters.title: Negotiation
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. He answers the encrypted offer, proposing a trade: the ledger for a new identity abroad and the deletion of every record tying him to the Halvern case. The buyer agrees — and sends proof-of-life stakes: a photo of Dana, taken this morning. Beat: the cost of the trade made flesh.

chapters.title: Counterfeit Ledger
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV, with Nadia assisting. Working from her kitchen table, he fabricates a convincing decoy ledger while preserving the original's authentication marks for investigators. Beat: purpose replacing panic; the investigator returns to work, off the books.

chapters.title: The Exchange at Pier 9
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. The midnight exchange goes sideways: the buyer intends to take both ledger and witness. Orsen springs his counter-trap — a live feed to a journalist and a dead-man switch. Beat: climax ignites; the trade becomes a standoff.

chapters.title: Fire on the Water
chapters.summary: Multi-POV. The pier erupts — syndicate muscle, internal affairs, and Dana arriving uninvited. Dana takes a bullet shielding Orsen; the decoy ledger burns; the journalist's feed captures the deputy director's arrival and arrest order in real time. Beat: sacrifice and chaos at peak tension.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. In a federal hearing room, Orsen speaks his real name aloud for the first time in nine years and authenticates the true ledger. The pipeline collapses; arrests ripple upward. Beat: catharsis through visibility — the thing he feared most saves everyone.

chapters.title: What the Money Bought
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Aftermath: Dana survives, recovering; the Unit is restructured; Orsen is offered a new identity anywhere in the world. He declines. Beat: the inheritance theme inverted — what he inherited from Halvern was not the file but the duty.

chapters.title: Sold
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. The safe house finally sells, legitimately, to a young family. Orsen walks through it one last time as a buyer's agent shows him out, and leaves the door unlocked behind him. Beat: release; the past closed gently rather than violently.

chapters.title: Felix and the Drop
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV, epilogue. Living openly under his own name, he joins Nadia's Sunday dinners and mentors a young investigator who reminds him of who he was. The final image: rain falling on a street where everyone knows his name, and he stays. Beat: belonging chosen, earned, and kept.
